levels.title: First light
levels.concept: Cross-zone traffic must pass a conduit, and the conduit permits only named flows.

paragraphs: You are the OT network engineer at a small electric co-op. In ISA/IEC 62443, a zone groups assets that have common security requirements, and a conduit is a grouping of the communication channels between zones. On this board, the Control Center and the Substation are zones, and the cell where they meet is the conduit that holds your firewall.

The SCADA master (M) in the Control Center sends requests and commands to RTUs (DNP3 outstations) in the Substation, and they send back data. Port 20000 is the registered DNP3 port. In this game the RTU listens on TCP port 20000 and the master opens the connection.

The standard defines security levels from SL 0 to SL 4. SL 2 protects against intentional attacks using simple means; SL 3 against sophisticated means with moderate resources. In this game each zone has a target security level (SL-T), and SL-T 2 means the conduit must deny by default and permit only named source → destination → service flows. Anything you don't permit is dropped by the implicit deny at the end of the rule list.

Write rule cards on the conduit, then press Run Wave. The wave shows sample traffic, but your policy is graded against every possible flow: it must permit exactly what the ticket asks for, and nothing more.
briefing.workedExample: Example (not one of the rounds): a water utility's historian (HS) in an Operations zone must read a pump controller (P1) in a Pump Station zone over DNP3. A least-privilege SL-T 2 policy is one card: permit HS → P1 tcp/20000. A card such as 'permit Operations → Pump Station any' would also let every other Operations host reach every pump-station device on every port, so it fails.
simplifications: Giving each zone an SL-T and turning it into firewall rules (SL-T 2 = deny by default with named flows) is this game's simplification, not a rule taken from the standard.
The master opening every TCP connection to the RTU's port 20000 is this game's model of DNP3 over TCP. Real devices can be set up in other ways.
Assets are identified by IP address only; DNP3 link-layer addresses are not modelled.
The firewall is stateful: replies on a connection you permitted return automatically.

rounds.title: First poll
rounds.ticketText: Work order 1.1: Cedar Creek is energized. The SCADA master (M) must poll Feeder 1's RTU (R1) over DNP3 so the operators can see the hospital feeder.
hints: Method: write down the ticket's flow as source → destination → service, then permit exactly that. Everything else is already denied by the implicit deny.
Worked step: the source is the SCADA master M and the destination is R1. DNP3 runs on TCP port 20000, so the service is tcp/20000 (or DNP3 with READ).
Reference rules: 1 permit M → R1 tcp/20000

feedback.correct: Exactly least privilege. The only new connection your conduit permits is the master polling R1 on TCP 20000, and the poll response returns inside that connection. The HMI's direct poll and the telnet attempt both hit the implicit deny.
feedback.required-blocked: The ticket flow {flow} was blocked at conduit {conduit} by {rule}, so the master can't poll the feeder. Add a permit for exactly this flow above any deny that matches it.
feedback.wrong-conduit: The ticket flow {flow} is permitted on part of its path but blocked at conduit {conduit} by {rule}. Permit it on every conduit it crosses.
feedback.attack-allowed: {flow} got through conduit {conduit} via {rule}, and that traffic isn't on the ticket. Narrow the source, destination or service so only the ticketed flow matches.
feedback.over-permissive: Your rules permit {count} cross-zone flow(s) the ticket doesn't need, for example {flow} via {rule} at conduit {conduit}. At SL-T 2 every permitted flow must be named; zone-wide or 'any' permits are too broad.

rounds.title: Second feeder
rounds.ticketText: Work order 1.2: Feeder 2 is back from maintenance. Keep your rule for R1 and add what the master (M) needs to poll Feeder 2's RTU (R2) over DNP3.

wave.label: HMI sending a control directly to R2
R1 probing R2 inside the substation
wave.explanation: R1 and R2 are both in the Substation zone, so this packet never crossed conduit A and no rule you write there can see it. A conduit only controls traffic between zones. To control traffic inside a zone you need something else: for example, split it into smaller zones with a conduit between them, or add controls inside the zone.

hints: Method: your R1 rule is already on the conduit. There is one new ticket flow; add one narrow permit for it rather than widening the rule you have.
Worked step: the new card has the same source and service as your R1 card, but the destination is R2.
Reference rules: 1 permit M → R1 tcp/20000; 2 permit M → R2 tcp/20000

feedback.correct: Exactly least privilege: two named flows, nothing else. The HMI's direct control of R2 hit the implicit deny. See the out-of-reach note for packet #4.
feedback.required-blocked: The ticket flow {flow} was blocked at conduit {conduit} by {rule}. Add a permit for exactly this flow above any deny that matches it.
feedback.wrong-conduit: The ticket flow {flow} is permitted on part of its path but blocked at conduit {conduit} by {rule}. A flow that crosses two conduits must be permitted on both: add a matching permit on conduit {conduit}.
feedback.attack-allowed: {flow} got through conduit {conduit} via {rule}, and that traffic isn't on the ticket. Narrow the rule so only ticketed traffic matches.
feedback.over-permissive: Your rules permit {count} cross-zone flow(s) the ticket doesn't need, for example {flow} via {rule} at conduit {conduit}. A zone-to-zone or 'any' permit covers both RTUs, but it also covers the HMI and every service. Name each flow instead.

levels.teaches: Zones, conduits and least privilege: permit exactly the flows the work order names, and let the implicit deny stop everything else.
levels.story: It's your first week at Prairie Ridge Electric Cooperative, and the new Cedar Creek substation energizes at dawn. Eleven thousand homes, the county hospital and the water plant hang off its feeders, and the only thing between them and the control center network is your conduit.

levels.title: Who calls whom
levels.concept: Only the master initiates DNP3 sessions; a stateful conduit returns replies and unsolicited responses inside them.

paragraphs: In this game's model of DNP3 over TCP, the master opens the connection to the RTU's port 20000. The RTU answers on that same connection, and it can also send unsolicited responses (function code 0x82) on it, for example to report an alarm without waiting to be asked.

Your conduit firewall is stateful. Once it permits a new connection, everything that belongs to that connection, including replies and unsolicited responses, comes back without any extra rule. Rules only decide who may open a new connection.
So in this model a rule from an RTU to the master is never needed. If you add one, you let a compromised RTU, or anything else in the Substation, start its own connections into the Control Center.
briefing.workedExample: Example (not one of the rounds): a web browser in an office opens a connection to a server, and the stateful office firewall lets the server's replies return. Nobody writes a rule allowing the server to open connections back to the browser. DNP3 polling works the same way: the master is the client.
simplifications: SL-T 2 still means deny by default with named flows (this game's simplification).
Set-ups where the outstation opens the TCP connection are not modelled.
The firewall tracks connections but does not simulate TCP itself.

rounds.title: The night-shift rule
rounds.ticketText: Work order 2.1: R1 and R2 now send unsolicited alarms. Your Level 1 rules are on conduit A, plus rule 3, which the night shift added so "the alarms can get through". The master (M) must keep polling R1 and R2, and every alarm must still reach M. Review the conduit.

wave.label: Master opens the session and polls R1
Compromised R1 opens its own connection to M

hints: Method: ask which side opens the connection. Only that direction needs a rule; the stateful conduit returns everything inside the connection, unsolicited alarms included.
Worked step: rules 1 and 2 let the master open both sessions, and the alarms (0x82) ride back inside them. Rule 3 only lets the Substation open new connections to M. Delete it.
Reference rules: 1 permit M → R1 tcp/20000; 2 permit M → R2 tcp/20000

feedback.correct: Exactly least privilege. Both alarms (0x82) came back inside the master's sessions with no inbound rule, and the compromised R1's attempt to open its own connection hit the implicit deny. The night-shift rule was a hole, not a fix.
feedback.required-blocked: The ticket flow {flow} was blocked at conduit {conduit} by {rule}. Add a permit for exactly this flow above any deny that matches it.
feedback.wrong-conduit: The ticket flow {flow} is permitted on part of its path but blocked at conduit {conduit} by {rule}. A flow that crosses two conduits must be permitted on both: add a matching permit on conduit {conduit}.
feedback.attack-allowed: {flow} opened a new connection through conduit {conduit} via {rule}. In this game's DNP3 model the master opens every session and unsolicited responses (0x82) return inside it, so this direction is never needed. Remove the Substation-to-master permit.
feedback.over-permissive: Your rules permit {count} cross-zone flow(s) the ticket doesn't need, for example {flow} via {rule} at conduit {conduit}. Permit only what the ticket names.

rounds.title: Wall display and a stranger
rounds.ticketText: Work order 2.2: the operators' new wall display (HMI, H) must read Feeder 2's RTU (R2) directly; it must not reach R1. Keep the master's polling. Security also reports an unknown device (X) plugged in at Cedar Creek.

wave.label: Unsolicited alarm from R2 to the display
Display reaching for R1 (not on the ticket)
Unknown device X tries to reach the master
Unknown device X scans the master
HMI forging the master's address to reach R1
wave.explanation: The HMI may not reach R1, so it forged the master's address. At conduit A the packet looked exactly like the permitted M → R1 poll, and no conduit rule can tell them apart. DNP3 Secure Authentication (IEEE 1815-2012, Chapter 7) lets an outstation challenge a critical request and act on it only if it was genuinely sent by a legitimate user. On the network side, switch features such as IP Source Guard only accept the source addresses bound to each access port, which limits a host's ability to claim another host's address.

hints: Method: rules 1 and 2 already cover the master. Add one permit for the new ticket flow, in the direction the display opens. Nothing in the Substation needs to open connections to the Control Center.
Worked step: the new card is H → R2 on tcp/20000. Don't widen it to the Substation zone: the display must not reach R1.
Reference rules: 1 permit M → R1 tcp/20000; 2 permit M → R2 tcp/20000; 3 permit H → R2 tcp/20000

feedback.correct: Exactly least privilege. The display reads R2 and nothing else, R2's alarm came back inside the display's session, and device X was denied. See the out-of-reach note for packet #6: least privilege at the conduit is necessary, but it is not the whole defence.
feedback.required-blocked: The ticket flow {flow} was blocked at conduit {conduit} by {rule}. Add a permit for exactly this flow above any deny that matches it.
feedback.wrong-conduit: The ticket flow {flow} is permitted on part of its path but blocked at conduit {conduit} by {rule}. A flow that crosses two conduits must be permitted on both: add a matching permit on conduit {conduit}.
feedback.attack-allowed: {flow} got through conduit {conduit} via {rule}, and that traffic isn't on the ticket. Name the exact source and destination; the display may read R2 only, and nothing in the Substation opens connections to the Control Center.
feedback.over-permissive: Your rules permit {count} cross-zone flow(s) the ticket doesn't need, for example {flow} via {rule} at conduit {conduit}. Permit only what the ticket names.

levels.teaches: Stateful conduits and DNP3 direction: the master opens every session, replies and unsolicited alarms ride back inside it, and an RTU-to-master rule is a hole.
levels.story: A January cold snap has every heater in the county running, and Cedar Creek's RTUs are firing alarms faster than the night shift can read them. Someone "fixed" the alarm traffic with a quick firewall rule, and now anything in the substation can call the master.

levels.title: Function codes and two conduits
levels.concept: At SL-T 3 the conduit inspects DNP3 and permits only the function codes each flow needs, on every conduit the flow crosses.

paragraphs: After the Level 2 incident, the co-op raised the Substation's target security level to SL-T 3. A conduit enforces the higher SL-T of the two zones it joins, so conduit 2 (Control Center ↔ Substation) is now SL-T 3, while conduit 1 (Engineering ↔ Control Center) stays SL-T 2.

At SL-T 3 in this game, port 20000 is not enough. The conduit must check that the traffic really is DNP3 and permit only the function codes the ticket needs. READ (0x01) requests data. SELECT (0x03) and OPERATE (0x04) work as a pair: a device can refuse an OPERATE when no SELECT came first. DIRECT_OPERATE (0x05) is a separate control code, and in this game it stands for control without that select step. COLD_RESTART (0x0D) is the Cold Restart code.
Rules are checked top-down and the first match wins. A broad permit placed above a narrower deny means the deny never runs.

Engineering reaches the Substation only through the Control Center, so a flow from Engineering crosses conduit 1 and then conduit 2. It must be permitted on both, and each conduit is graded on its own.
briefing.workedExample: Example (not one of the rounds): a pump controller should only ever be read by the historian. At SL-T 3 the card is permit Historian → Pump DNP3 {READ}, not permit Historian → Pump tcp/20000, because the port-only card would also pass WRITE, DIRECT_OPERATE, COLD_RESTART, or a non-DNP3 tunnel on port 20000.
simplifications: SL-T 3 = DNP3 protocol check plus function-code filtering is this game's simplification, not a rule taken from the standard.
In this game, the ticket decides whether DIRECT_OPERATE is allowed.
Each forbidden flow must be denied at every conduit it crosses (defense in depth).

rounds.title: Raise the bar
rounds.ticketText: Work order 3.1: your Level 2 rules now sit on conduit 2, which is SL-T 3. Upgrade them. The master (M) must poll R1 and trip its breaker with select-before-operate (READ, SELECT, OPERATE), and keep reading R2. The display (H) still reads R2. Threat intel warns the master itself may be compromised.

wave.label: Display writing to R2 (not on the ticket)

hints: Method: at SL-T 3 a port-only permit is too broad. Change each card's service to DNP3 and tick only the function codes its ticket line names. One card can carry several codes.
Worked step: rule 1 becomes M → R1 DNP3 with READ, SELECT and OPERATE ticked. That also stops the non-DNP3 tunnel, because it isn't DNP3.
Reference rules, on conduit 2: 1 permit M → R1 DNP3 {READ, SELECT, OPERATE}; 2 permit M → R2 DNP3 {READ}; 3 permit H → R2 DNP3 {READ}

feedback.correct: Exactly least privilege. The master can poll and use select-before-operate, but even a compromised master cannot DIRECT_OPERATE or COLD_RESTART R1. The display can only READ R2, and the port-20000 tunnel failed the DNP3 protocol check. Function-code filtering limits what a trusted address can do.
feedback.required-blocked: The ticket flow {flow} was blocked at conduit {conduit} by {rule}. Add a permit for exactly this flow above any deny that matches it.
feedback.wrong-conduit: The ticket flow {flow} is permitted on part of its path but blocked at conduit {conduit} by {rule}. A flow that crosses two conduits must be permitted on both: add a matching permit on conduit {conduit}.
feedback.attack-allowed: {flow} got through conduit {conduit} via {rule}. Port 20000 or 'any FC' lets dangerous function codes through, even from a trusted address. Switch each card to DNP3 with only the ticketed codes, and check the order of your rules: the first match wins.
feedback.over-permissive: Your rules permit {count} flow(s) the ticket doesn't need, for example {flow} via {rule} at conduit {conduit}. At SL-T 3 both the function code and the protocol check count: a port-only or 'any FC' permit is too broad.

rounds.title: Two conduits
rounds.ticketText: Work order 3.2: the master (M) must also DIRECT_OPERATE R2's capacitor bank (the co-op allows direct control for this device only). The engineering workstation (E) must read R2's event logs. A vendor laptop (V) is also on the Engineering network. Keep everything from 3.1.

wave.label: Direct control of R1 (not on the ticket)

hints: Method: two ticket lines changed. Add DIRECT_OPERATE to the card that already covers M → R2. Then trace the new Engineering flow: it crosses conduit 1 and then conduit 2, so it needs a permit on both.
Worked step: on conduit 2, tick DIRECT_OPERATE on rule 2 and add E → R2 DNP3 {READ}. Then switch to conduit 1 (SL-T 2) and permit E → R2.

Reference rules. Conduit 1: 1 permit E → R2 tcp/20000. Conduit 2: 1 permit M → R1 DNP3 {READ, SELECT, OPERATE}; 2 permit M → R2 DNP3 {READ, DIRECT_OPERATE}; 3 permit H → R2 DNP3 {READ}; 4 permit E → R2 DNP3 {READ}

feedback.correct: Exactly least privilege across two conduits. Engineering's log read crossed both conduits, the capacitor bank can be switched directly, and DIRECT_OPERATE to R1 is still blocked, because the ticket, not the function code, defines what is allowed. The vendor laptop stopped at conduit 1.
feedback.required-blocked: The ticket flow {flow} was blocked at conduit {conduit} by {rule}. Add a permit for exactly this flow above any deny that matches it.
feedback.wrong-conduit: The ticket flow {flow} is permitted on part of its path but blocked at conduit {conduit} by {rule}. A flow that crosses two conduits must be permitted on both: add a matching permit on conduit {conduit}.
feedback.attack-allowed: {flow} got through conduit {conduit} via {rule}. The same function code can be required for one device and forbidden for another; name the destination as well as the codes.
feedback.over-permissive: Your rules permit {count} cross-zone flow(s) the ticket doesn't need, for example {flow} via {rule} at conduit {conduit}. Permit only what the ticket names.

levels.teaches: SL-T 3 and DNP3 function codes: filter on what a flow may do, not just its port, and permit a flow on every conduit it crosses.
levels.story: After the winter incident the board raised Cedar Creek to SL-T 3, and the auditors arrive Friday. A vendor's laptop sits on the engineering bench, a capacitor bank needs remote switching, and every function code you allow is a breaker someone could trip.
